title: Backgrounds
text: This page covers the three kinds of background, how the text color adapts to them, and how to set a background for one slide or for the whole deck.

title: Backgrounds
text:
Three kinds
Background has one constructor per kind:







Constructor
Paints




Background.color(c)
One CSS color.


Background.gradient(start, end, mid=None, angle=135)
A linear gradient of two or three colors, at an angle in degrees.


Background.image(src, overlay="rgba(0,0,0,0.55)")
A photo from a URL, a file path or bytes, under a dark overlay.



from banners import Background, Section, Text

Section(
    title="Solid color",
    content=[Text("The text turns white on a dark color.")],
    background=Background.color("#0f172a"),
)
from banners import Background, Section, Text

Section(
    title="Gradient",
    content=[Text("Two or three stops at any angle.")],
    background=Background.gradient("#1e3a5f", "#6d28d9", angle=135),
)
# fragment: downloads the photo when the background is created.
from banners import Background, Section, Text

Section(
    title="Photo",
    content=[Text("A dark overlay keeps the text readable.")],
    background=Background.image(
        "https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/"
        "Pillars_of_creation_2014_HST_WFC3-UVIS_full-res_denoised.jpg?width=1600"
    ),
)






Color







Gradient







Photo

title: Backgrounds
text:
The text adapts
banners reads the first color of the background and measures how light it is. On a dark background the text and subtitles turn white; on a light one they stay dark. That is why a dark gradient needs no change to the palette. The title keeps the palette’s primary color unless it would be hard to read.
For a photo, the overlay decides: the default dark overlay makes the text white. overlay=None removes it; banners then cannot measure the photo, so the text keeps the palette colors, and a dark photo may need a palette with light text.

title: Backgrounds
section: One slide or the whole deck
text:
One slide or the whole deck
background= on a slide paints that slide. configure(background=...) paints every slide that does not set its own:
from banners import Background, configure

configure(background=Background.gradient("#0f172a", "#1e3a5f"))
A photo given by URL is downloaded once, when the background is created, and embedded in the slides. The download checks the server’s certificate; a failed download raises an error instead of producing a blank slide.

title: Templates
text: This page covers what a template is, the six templates that come with banners, and the options that a template of your own can set.

title: Templates
section: One line changes the whole deck
text:
One line changes the whole deck
A template draws every slide of the deck. The slides only hold their content (titles, text, plots); the template decides where each piece goes and which colors and fonts it uses. That is why one call changes the look of a whole presentation:
from banners import EXECUTIVE, configure

configure(template=EXECUTIVE)
Every slide created after this call uses EXECUTIVE. Without a call to configure(template=...), banners uses Template(), the default template.

title: Templates
text:
The built-in templates
The same slide drawn with each template:






Template() — the default: light slides, orange titles.







EXECUTIVE — white, black serif titles, chart mark.









INSTITUTIONAL — navy and pale blue, serif titles.







COSMOS — dark slides, cyan, violet and pink, space photos.









VIBRANT — white, a four-color bar and a different color per section.







TERRA — warm sand background, forest green, landscape photos.





All of them are importable from banners:
from banners import COSMOS, EXECUTIVE, INSTITUTIONAL, TERRA, VIBRANT, Template

title: Templates
section: What a template is made of
text:
What a template is made of
A Template combines three things:

Layouts: where the title, the content, the logo and the bottom bar go on each kind of slide. They are built into banners; the Layouts page shows how a slide picks one.
A Palette: the colors, by role (title, text, background, bar…). See Palettes.
A Theme: fonts, title weight, icon stroke and a size multiplier. See Themes.

On top of those, a template can carry logos, pictures and a few switches:







Option
What it does




logo_on_dark, logo_on_light
Logo drawn on dark slides (cover, closing) and on light ones. A URL, a file path or raw bytes.


mark
Small symbol in the top-right corner of content slides: an image or an icon name such as "chart".


cover_image, divider_image
Photo used by every cover, or every divider, unless the slide sets its own.


divider_icon
Large icon on dividers without a photo.


closing_image
Picture next to the closing title.


bar, bar_split
Draw the two-color bar along the bottom edge, and how much of it is the primary color.


auto_contrast
Replace a title color that would be hard to read on its background. Turn it off to keep exact brand colors.



Images given as URLs are loaded by the browser when the slide is shown; paths and bytes are embedded in the slide.

title: Templates
text:
A template of your own
A template is a plain Python object, so a deck can define its own in a notebook cell and use it with configure():
from banners import Palette, Template, Theme, configure

ours = Template(
    palette=Palette(primary="#0f766e", secondary="#f59e0b"),
    theme=Theme(heading_font="Georgia, serif"),
    mark="chart",
)
configure(template=ours, team="Data Office", date="2026")
Your organization’s template builds a complete one, with logos.

title: Templates
section: Changing only the colors or the fonts
text:
Changing only the colors or the fonts
To keep a template’s layouts and change only its colors or fonts, pass a palette or a theme to configure() instead of building a new template:
from banners import BLUE, COSMOS, configure

configure(template=COSMOS, palette=BLUE)
The palette given to configure() replaces the template’s palette as a whole. The next pages explain palettes and themes in detail.

title: Cache and speed
text: This guide covers the render cache of Manim and FlowAnimation and the settings that keep a deck quick to open.

title: Cache and speed
text:
Where the cache lives
The first time a cell with an animation runs, Manim renders it, which takes from one to a few seconds. banners stores the result in
~/.cache/banners/manim/
and later runs read it from there at once, also after restarting marimo.

title: Cache and speed
section: When an animation is rendered again

title: Cache and speed
text:
Clear the cache
Deleting the folder is safe; animations are rendered again when needed:
rm -rf ~/.cache/banners/manim

title: Cache and speed
text:
Keep a deck fast

Work in quality="low" and switch to "medium" or "high" for the final version only.
Prefer interactive=True or format="mp4" to long GIFs. A GIF stores every frame as an image: a few seconds at high quality can weigh tens of megabytes and exceed marimo’s output limit, which then shows “Your output is too large” instead of the animation. MP4 is a fraction of that size.
Render once before the talk, so every animation comes from the cache during the presentation.

title: A click-through Manim scene
text: This guide writes a Manim scene for a talk: steps that follow the speaker, short and direct motion, and colors that match the slide.

title: A click-through Manim scene
text:
One step per idea
self.next_section() starts a new step. With Manim(..., interactive=True), each step waits for a click, so the speaker decides when the next idea appears:
from banners import BLUE, Manim, Section
from manim import DOWN, RIGHT, Arrow, FadeIn, GrowArrow, RoundedRectangle, Scene, VGroup, rate_functions
from manim import Text as MText

class Pipeline(Scene):
    def construct(self):
        names = ["Ingest", "Clean", "Train"]
        boxes = VGroup(*[
            VGroup(
                RoundedRectangle(width=2.4, height=1, corner_radius=0.12,
                                 color=BLUE.primary, fill_opacity=0.15),
                MText(name, font_size=26, color=BLUE.text),
            )
            for name in names
        ]).arrange(RIGHT, buff=1.2)
        for i, box in enumerate(boxes):
            self.next_section(f"step_{i}")
            parts = [FadeIn(box, shift=RIGHT * 0.15)]
            if i:
                parts.append(GrowArrow(Arrow(boxes[i - 1].get_right(), box.get_left(),
                                             buff=0.1, color=BLUE.muted)))
            self.play(*parts, run_time=0.25, rate_func=rate_functions.ease_out_cubic)

Section(title="Our pipeline", content=[Manim(Pipeline, interactive=True)], palette=BLUE)

title: A click-through Manim scene
section: Rules that make a scene present well
text:
Rules that make a scene present well

One change per click. Each step shows one new idea; the audience reads it while the speaker talks.
Short steps. Between 0.2 and 0.4 seconds per step, with an ease-out curve (rate_functions.ease_out_cubic): the motion starts fast and settles. Long animations make the audience wait for the slide.
No pause at the end. A step ends when its motion ends; a trailing self.wait() only delays the next click.
No decoration. Every element on screen is part of the explanation.
The slide’s colors. Do not set self.camera.background_color: banners draws the scene on the slide’s panel color. Take the colors of shapes and text from the palette, as BLUE.primary and BLUE.text above.

Names that clash with banners
banners and Manim both export Text, and Manim’s color constants (such as BLUE) share names with the banners palettes. Import Manim’s under another name, as from manim import Text as MText above, so a marimo notebook does not see two definitions of the same name.

title: A click-through Manim scene
text:
Scenes that follow any palette
A function that takes palette and returns a Scene class receives the slide’s palette from banners:
from banners import Manim, Section
from manim import Circle, Create, Scene

def Dot(palette):
    class _Dot(Scene):
        def construct(self):
            self.play(Create(Circle(color=palette.primary)), run_time=0.3)
    return _Dot

Section(title="Follows the slide", content=[Manim(Dot)])
